chunks: Muhammad ibn Aqeel from Al-Hasan ibn Al-Husayn, from Ali ibn Isa, from Ali ibn Al-Hasan, from Muhammad ibn Yazeed Al-Rifa'i, raising it (to the Imam).

That the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) was asked about the standing at the Mountain (Jabal al-Rahmah), why it was not in the Sanctuary (Haram)? So he said: 'Because the Ka'bah is His House and the Haram is its door. So when they came to it as delegates, He stopped them at the door, supplicating.'

It was said to him: 'So why has Al-Mashar Al-Haram become inside the Haram?' He said: 'Because when He permitted them to enter, He stopped them at the second Veil. So when their supplication at it was prolonged, He permitted them to offer their sacrifice. So when they fulfilled their minor rituals, they were purified by it from the sins which were a veil between them and Him. He permitted them the visitation upon purity.'

It was said to him: 'So why was fasting prohibited during the Days of Tashreeq?' He said: 'Because the people are visitors of Allah, and they are in His hospitality, and it is not fitting for a Host that He should make His guests fast.'

It was said to him: 'So what is the meaning of hanging onto the curtains of the Ka'bah?' He said: 'It is like a man who has a felony and a sin with another, so he hangs onto his garment, supplicating to him and humbling himself to him that he would overlook his sin.'

key_terms.أَيَّامُ التَّشْرِيقِ: The Days of Tashreeq (11th, 12th, 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah)
key_terms.الْمَشْعَرُ الْحَرَامُ: Al-Mashar Al-Haram (the sacred site at Muzdalifah)

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual and legal reasoning behind the Hajj rituals and the prohibition of fasting during Tashreeq?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam Ali (peace be upon him) elucidates the metaphysical wisdom behind Hajj rituals, framing the pilgrim's journey as a progression from the 'door' (Arafat) to the 'curtain' (Muzdalifah) and finally into the divine presence. It interprets the prohibition of fasting during Tashreeq as an act of divine hospitality, where God, as the host, does not weary His guests, while the act of touching the Ka'bah's curtains symbolizes a sinner's humble supplication for pardon. This narrative reinforces the Shia emphasis on the spiritual dimensions of ritual acts (ma'ani) alongside their legal forms (ahkam).
